questions.question: What does fmt.Errorf with %w do?
questions.title: Fmt.errorf With %w Do
questions.direct_answer: Creates an error that wraps another error — adding your message while keeping errors.Is/As working through the chain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Fmt Errorf beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: Creates an error that wraps another error — adding your message while keeping errors.Is/As working through the chain.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
%w is the wrap verb. It builds a new error whose message is your formatted text with the wrapped error's message embedded, AND records the wrapped error as unwrap-able:

```go
base := errors.New("disk full")
wrapped := fmt.Errorf("write config: %w", base)

// prints: write config: disk full
// AND: errors.Is(wrapped, base) == true — the chain is intact
```

That second property is the whole point. Any caller can ask 'was the underlying cause disk full?' and get the right answer, no matter how many layers wrapped it. Without %w — with %v — the message would print the same, but the causal link would be severed: the chain is data the error carries, not text.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B[base error] --> W1[fmt.Errorf %w — chain edge]
    W1 --> W2[another %w wrap — context added]
    W2 --> IS[errors.Is walks the chain — finds base]
    W1 --> AS[errors.As extracts types through it]
    V[%v instead] --> CUT[chain severed — Is fails]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Mechanically, %w tells fmt.Errorf to store the wrapped error in the returned error's internal tree (an fmt.wrapError holding both your format result and the cause). The errors package's Is and As walk that tree via Unwrap: each %w is an edge, and Is/As traverse edges until they find a match or exhaust the chain.

The walk semantics are the interview-grade detail:

- errors.Is(e, target) — walks the chain, comparing each node to target (identity or the target's Is method). True if the cause is anywhere below.
- errors.As(e, &typedTarget) — walks until it finds an error assignable to the type, then copies it into your target.
- Both treat the chain as read-only evidence: they never unwrap past a %v (there's no edge to follow).

The composed behavior — wrap at every layer with %w, inspect with Is/As at the boundary — is Go's answer to exception type-matching, but with the chain explicit in the data rather than in a type hierarchy.

questions.question: %w vs %v in error messages — what is the practical difference?
questions.title: %w Vs %v In Error Messages —
questions.direct_answer: They print identically. %w preserves the unwrap chain (errors.Is/As work); %v bakes the text in and cuts the chain.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: They print identically.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The two lines look the same and behave differently:

```go
base := errors.New("disk full")
withW := fmt.Errorf("write config: %w", base)
withV := fmt.Errorf("write config: %v", base)

// both print: "write config: disk full"

errors.Is(withW, base)   // true
errors.Is(withV, base)   // false — the chain is gone
```

%w stores the cause as a linkable edge; %v renders the cause's message into the string at construction and keeps no reference. The information content of the message is identical — the difference is entirely whether the machine can still ask questions about the cause.

So the rule: %w whenever a caller below you might need to match or extract the cause (which is most wrapping — you rarely know your caller's needs). %v when the error is headed for a human log line and no code will inspect it — a top-level 'failed to start: %v' that nothing branches on.

The bug shape to recognize: someone 'cleaned up' %w to %v for style, and six months later a caller's errors.Is quietly became always-false. The test that would catch it is a test on the wrap — which most codebases never write.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    X[option 1] --> AXIS[same axis of comparison]
    Y[option 2] --> AXIS
    AXIS --> PICK[the rule that decides]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The printed output is byte-identical; the internal structure is completely different. It's worth seeing once what %v actually does to the cause:

%v calls the cause's Error() method AT FORMAT TIME and interpolates the string. The resulting wrapError holds your formatted text — the cause's message is now embedded characters, and the cause value itself was discarded after formatting. The chain ends: Unwrap() on the result has nothing to return.

%w stores the cause as a field. The message is built the same way (the cause's text appears identically), but the wrapError also implements Unwrap() -> cause. The errors package's Is/As walk that edge.

So the mental model: both verbs render the cause's MESSAGE; only %w preserves the cause's IDENTITY. Text vs identity is the whole difference — and every downstream question (Is this a DiskFull? What's the RateLimit's duration?) is an identity question. Answers that require identity need %w; answers satisfied by prose don't.

The migration trap: codebases that started %v-everywhere (or pre-1.13, before %w existed) have wraps that LOOK chainable but aren't. errors.Is through them is silently false. The audit is mechanical — grep for Errorf calls with %v and an err argument, and check each: terminal-format (fine) or chain-middle (should be %w).

questions.question: Can you wrap multiple errors with fmt.Errorf?
questions.title: Can You Wrap Multiple Errors With Fmt.errorf
questions.direct_answer: Not with %w — exactly one. Go 1.20's errors.Join(err1, err2) wraps several into one error that Is-matches each component.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Not with %w — exactly one.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B[base error] --> W1[fmt.Errorf %w — chain edge]
    W1 --> W2[another %w wrap — context added]
    W2 --> IS[errors.Is walks the chain — finds base]
    W1 --> AS[errors.As extracts types through it]
    V[%v instead] --> CUT[chain severed — Is fails]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
errors.Join is the 1.20 answer to a pattern the community had already reinvented several times (hashicorp/go-multierror, the multierr libraries) — and the standard library's version has one API decision those didn't: it's an error, not an errors-collection API. You return it like any error; callers who don't care see one error with a newline-joined message.

The semantics that make Join correct (and hand-rolled versions subtly wrong):

- Is: joined matches a target if ANY component matches — callers still find sentinels inside batches.
- As: extracts the first component of the requested type — the caller gets typed data out of a many-failure return.
- Unwrap() []error: the Go 1.20 multi-edge — Is/As treat a []error unwrap as a branch, walking every branch. The subtle part older versions got wrong: walking a tree (Join of Joins) without double-visiting or missing branches. The stdlib's tree-walk is the tested one.

- nil handling: Join drops nil components, and Join() of all-nils returns nil — the builder pattern (collect errs, Join at the end) needs no guard.

When NOT to use it: sequential failure (step 2 didn't run because step 1 failed) — return the first error; joining implies 'all of these were attempted and failed,' which would be fiction. Join is for genuine parallelism: batch validation, fan-out requests, per-field form errors. The message shape tells the story: a Join prints as a list; a sequential chain prints as a narrative.

questions.question: When should you add context with Errorf instead of returning err directly?
questions.title: N Should You Add Context With Errorf
questions.direct_answer: When your layer adds meaning the caller can't infer: the operation, the file, the request. If the error already says everything, pass it through.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: When your layer adds meaning the caller can't infer: the operation, the file, the request.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B[base error] --> W1[fmt.Errorf %w — chain edge]
    W1 --> W2[another %w wrap — context added]
    W2 --> IS[errors.Is walks the chain — finds base]
    W1 --> AS[errors.As extracts types through it]
    V[%v instead] --> CUT[chain severed — Is fails]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The decision has a precise test, and it's about the READER's first question. When a caller sees an error from your function, the question is always 'what was happening?' — and the answer must be derivable from the error's chain. If your layer knows the answer and the chain doesn't carry it, wrap. If the chain already implies it, pass through.

The naming connection is the deep one: well-factored code needs LESS error context, because the function name carries it. `loadConfig()` returning a wrapped open-file error adds 'load config:' — but if the caller got that from calling loadConfig, they know that already. The wrap earns its line when the fact is otherwise invisible:

- a path the caller passed in (they know it — maybe skip)
- an INTERNAL path the caller never saw (they don't know it — wrap)
- which of several attempts failed (retry number, shard index — wrap)
- a value that matters to the failure (limit exceeded: N — wrap)

The read-aloud test: every segment should add a fact. 'failed, because: start server: listen :8080: address in use' — the 'failed because' segment never does.

Practical consequence: context belongs at the layer that HAS the fact, not the layer that noticed the failure. The deepest error knows the syscall; the top knows the operation; each layer adds its own fact and no one else's. That's how a well-wrapped chain reads like a debugging narrative without any layer guessing about others.

questions.question: What does errors.Is do with a wrapped chain?
questions.title: Rrors.is Do With A Wrapped Chain
questions.direct_answer: Walks the Unwrap chain comparing each error to the target. fmt.Errorf %w links the chain; Is finds the sentinel anywhere inside.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Walks the Unwrap chain comparing each error to the target.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
errors.Is is the chain-aware equality check:

```go
var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")

err := fmt.Errorf("get user: %w", ErrNotFound)

errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)   // true — found through the wrap
err == ErrNotFound            // false — they're different values
```

The walk: Is takes the error and follows Unwrap edges — each %w is one edge — comparing each node against the target with == (or the target's Is method, if it has one). The sentinel can sit any number of wraps deep; Is finds it because the chain is traversable data.

This is why Is replaced raw == for sentinels: == sees only the top value (the outermost wrap — not equal), while Is sees the whole causal history. A caller that uses == breaks the moment any intermediate layer wraps; a caller that uses Is survives arbitrary wrapping — which is exactly the compat contract between layers that don't know each other.

The As variant does the same walk for types: errors.As(err, &myErrTypedPointer) finds the first node assignable to the type and copies it out. Is for identities, As for types with fields — both powered by the same chain.

```mermaid
    W1 --> W2[another %w wrap — context added]
    W2 --> IS[errors.Is walks the chain — finds base]
    W1 --> AS[errors.As extracts types through it]
    V[%v instead] --> CUT[chain severed — Is fails]
```
